intended_object: A basic ring (or basic algebra): a ring A whose quotient A/J(A) by the Jacobson radical is a finite product of division rings. For a finite-dimensional algebra this is the same as A_A having no repeated indecomposable projective summand (Assem–Simson–Skowroński I.6). Source: the docstring and the module documentation.
explanation:
The body says that A ⧸ Ring.jacobson A is semisimple and reduced. Mathlib's `Ring.jacobson` is a two-sided ideal (it has an `IsTwoSided` instance), so the quotient is a ring. By Artin–Wedderburn, a semisimple ring is a finite product of matrix rings M_{n_i}(D_i) over division rings. Such a product is reduced exactly when every n_i = 1, because for n_i ≥ 2 the matrix unit E_{12} is a nonzero element with square zero. So the body is equivalent to "A/J(A) is a finite product of division rings", which the library proves as `isBasic_iff_pi_divisionRing`.

Both clauses are needed. Reducedness alone would make ℤ basic, since J(ℤ) = 0 and ℤ is reduced, and the module docs point this out.

The definition is stated for an arbitrary `Ring`, which is the most general natural setting. No base field and no finiteness is assumed.

One caveat: Lam and Anderson–Fuller define "basic" only for semiperfect rings. This definition also covers semilocal rings that are not semiperfect, for example the localization of ℤ at the complement of (2) ∪ (3), which counts as basic here. On semiperfect rings, and in particular on finite-dimensional algebras, it agrees exactly with the textbook notion. Outside them the textbook notion is not defined, so this is a natural extension rather than an error. Every use in the library is for finite-dimensional algebras or comes with a separate semiperfectness hypothesis.

Mathlib has no notion of basic ring.
